title: AI Newsletter #01 – Kolmogorov-Arnold Networks!
text:
Background and Introduction

Exploring the power of Kolmogorov-Arnold Networks for smarter, sharper function approximation.

Welcome to our first newsletter! We’ll start with a bit of background on the math and architecture behind KANs, then go through a KAN implementation. The GitHub repo for everything is linked at the end of the article. Along the way, we’ll share some interesting empirical results and try to build an intuition for how it all works. Hope you enjoy it!

The MLP architecture and limitations
Standard multi-layer perceptrons (MLPs) place fixed activation functions (ReLU, SiLU, etc.) inside the nodes. Linear transformations (weights) live on the edges. This architecture forces the network to approximate any target function by stitching together many global hyperplanes. This is an approach that works but is extremely parameter-inefficient for smooth, high-frequency, or compositional functions (eg. \(f(g(x))\)).
The KAN architecture and applications
KANs generated significant excitement in the ML community around 2024, as researchers recognized their potential to drastically improve function representation with fewer parameters and more interpretable structure. The hype was fueled by early benchmarks showing remarkably efficient interpolation, sparking interest in both theoretical exploration and practical applications.
Kolmogorov-Arnold Networks (KANs) achieve this by mitigating key limitations of traditional neural architectures. They eliminate fixed node activations entirely: every edge becomes a learnable univariate function φ, and every node simply sums its incoming signals. The entire network is thus a composition of univariate functions and summations, precisely the structure promised by the famous Kolmogorov-Arnold representation theorem.

title: AI Newsletter #01 – Kolmogorov-Arnold Networks!
text:
Unpacking the Theorem
The Kolmogorov-Arnold representation theorem (refined in the 1960s) states that any continuous multivariate function \(f: [0,1]^n \to \mathbb{R}\) can be written as:
\[f(\mathbf{x}) = \sum_{q=1}^{2n+1} \Phi_q \left( \sum_{p=1}^n \phi_{q,p}(x_p) \right)\]
That’s a fantastic guarantee, but throwing raw equations at a problem doesn’t help us write code. To make this useful, we need to map the math directly to a network architecture.

Inner edges \(\phi_{q,p}(x_p)\): Instead of mixing inputs right away like in an MLP, each input (\(x_p\)) is first passed through its own separate 1D function, completely independent of the others.
Intermediate nodes \(\sum_{p=1}^n\): After that, the transformed inputs are just added together. No activation here, just a sum.
Outer edges \(\Phi_q\): So how do we capture interactions like \(x_1 \cdot x_2\) if we only add things? That happens here. A final nonlinear 1D function is applied to the sum, which lets the model represent those interactions.
Hidden dimension \(2n+1\): This is the key guarantee. With \(n\) inputs, you only need \(2n+1\) of these nodes to represent any continuous function (e.g., 5 nodes for 2D input).

title: AI Newsletter #01 – Kolmogorov-Arnold Networks!
text:
Why KANs Matter
The Kolmogorov-Arnold theorem has been around since the 1950s. What changed is that we can now learn those univariate functions end-to-end with gradient descent, effectively turning a theoretical existence proof into a working architecture.
Where KANs shine

Scientific discovery and symbolic regression. Each edge is a univariate function, so you can prune the network and literally read off the learned expression, i.e. “this edge learned \(x²\), that one learned \(sin(3πx)\).” For physics, chemistry, and biology, that could be the foundation for new discoveries!
Physics and PDE solvers. KANs respect compositional structure naturally, so they extrapolate far better than MLPs when solving differential equations outside the training domain.
High-frequency and periodic phenomena. As the radial sine ripple demo will show later, KANs (especially SIREN-KAN variants) can capture rapid oscillations with far fewer parameters.
Low-to-medium dimensional problems. Financial time series, engineering simulations, control systems. Tasks with roughly 2–20 input dimensions, where interpretability and reliable extrapolation are important.

 They have been hyped, but is it justified?
MLPs approximate complex surfaces by overlapping vast numbers of flat hyperplanes. KANs follow the exact decomposition that the theorem guarantees exists, which gives them real structural advantages: often 10–100× fewer parameters on smooth functions, better out-of-distribution behavior, and interpretable edges you can inspect or symbolically regress.
MLPs are excellent for messy, high-dimensional data like images and text. KANs on the other hand are what you should apply when you suspect there’s an underlying mathematical law to be found.

title: AI Newsletter #01 – Kolmogorov-Arnold Networks!
text:
SIREN-KAN
The original KAN paper (Liu et al., 2024) parameterised the univariate edge functions \(\phi\) with B-splines. This choice gives excellent localisation and interpretability, but B-splines struggle with high-frequency oscillations (which is what we are going to be testing here!) because they are inherently low-pass (smooth polynomial pieces).
When people replace B-splines with tiny MLPs (a common simplification in early re-implementations), the network inherits the spectral bias of standard MLPs and fails to capture rapid oscillations.
 The SIREN-KAN solution
In this implementation we will replace the activation inside each edge with a SIREN-style periodic basis: \(sin(\omega_0 x + b)\). By scaling the first-layer frequencies with \(\omega_0\) and using careful initialisation, each univariate edge gains infinite periodic capacity. The result is a network that can learn the exact algebraic structure of high-frequency targets (e.g. sin(polynomial)) with dramatically fewer parameters.

title: AI Newsletter #01 – Kolmogorov-Arnold Networks!
text:
(Pseudo-) Code overview
This is the rough KAN architecture:
# full repo is separate (see bottom)

for layer in KAN_layers:
    
    # Inner univariate functions (one per edge)
    for every input_dim → hidden_dim edge:
        φ = sin(ω₀·x + b)               # SIREN-style
        edge_out = linear(φ)            # small projection
    h = sum(edge_out over input_dim)    # node sums
    
    # Outer univariate functions
    for every hidden_dim → out_dim edge:
        Φ = sin(ω₀·h + b)
        edge_out = linear(Φ)
    y = sum(edge_out over hidden_dim)

title: AI Newsletter #01 – Kolmogorov-Arnold Networks!
section: The Stress Test: High-Frequency Radial Ripples
text:
The Stress Test: High-Frequency Radial Ripples
Target function (chosen to be analytically simple yet extremely difficult for spectral-biased networks): \[
f(x_1, x_2) = \sin\bigl(3\pi(x_1^2 + x_2^2)\bigr)
\]
This is a radially symmetric sine wave whose frequency increases quadratically with distance from the origin, basically a perfect stress test for extrapolation.

title: AI Newsletter #01 – Kolmogorov-Arnold Networks!
text:
Experimental Setup
To rigorously evaluate whether these architectures actually learn the underlying mathematical rules, we analyzed performance within the training domain and also conducted a strict out-of-distribution (OOD) extrapolation test.

The Competitors: A standard Multi-Layer Perceptron (two 64-neuron hidden layers, ~4,400 parameters) relying on global hyperplanes, matched against our custom SIREN-KAN (hidden dimension of 5, ~375 parameters) equipped with localized, frequency-scaled sine activations.
The Training Domain (Interpolation): Both models were trained exclusively on uniformly sampled data within the boundary \(x_1, x_2 \in [-1.2, 1.2]\). This provides a solid, bounded view of the central concentric ripples.
The Testing Domain (Extrapolation): We then evaluated their predictive power on an expanded grid spanning \([-1.4, 1.4]\).

Why it matters: Neural networks are usually great at interpolating, but extrapolating? Not so much. If a network just memorizes the space by patching together overlapping linear segments (like a standard MLP), its predictions will fall apart as soon as you move past the \(1.2\) boundary.
On the other hand, if a network’s inductive bias really captures the underlying periodic pattern, the exact boundary shouldn’t matter. Our hypothesis was that the KAN would handle this out-of-domain prediction much better.

title: AI Newsletter #01 – Kolmogorov-Arnold Networks!
text:
Results






Figure 1: 3D Surface Comparison: The MLP struggles with high-frequency ripples while the KAN maps them very well.



The MLP shows a clear spectral bias: it handles the low-frequency, broad patterns near the origin pretty well, but completely misses the high-frequency details at the edges. The KAN, on the other hand, is much more expressive for this kind of problem, capturing both the coarse structure and the fine oscillations across the whole space.






Figure 2: Training Dynamics and Prediction Fidelity.



Training Dynamics (Left):
You can pretty clearly see the MLP struggling during training. It hits a plateau early and then keeps spiking all over the place, which is a classic sign that the optimizer is fighting itself trying to fit high-frequency signals with a rigid structure. The KAN, on the other hand, is much smoother. Around epoch ~450 it actually breaks through that plateau and keeps improving, ending up at a much lower MSE.
Prediction Fidelity (Right):
The scatter plot makes it even more obvious. The KAN predictions sit right around the dashed “perfect prediction” line across the whole range. The MLP is way more scattered. You can even see these horizontal bands (especially around y ≈ 0.25), which indicates that it has basically given up and is predicting constant values over big chunks of the input space. It’s not clearly capturing the structure of the data as well as the KAN.

Interpolation:
Within the training domain, the Kolmogorov-Arnold Network performs exceptionally well. It achieved a near-perfect MSE of 0.0014 compared to the MLP’s 0.1063, a 98.7% reduction in error. It achieves this while using roughly 12x fewer parameters, proving that its periodic 1D edges natively capture high-frequency ripples far better than the MLP’s overlapping global hyperplanes.
Extrapolation:
The out-of-distribution test reveals the true power of the architecture’s inductive bias. The MLP fails catastrophically (MSE 1.87). Because it merely memorized the spatial grid, it runs out of hyperplanes past the 1.2 boundary and predicts chaotic noise.
The SIREN-KAN, however, successfully holds its structural integrity outside the training bounds (MSE 0.29). By deeply converging on the correct phase alignments of its internal sine waves, it managed to parameterize the periodic-quadratic structure well enough to accurately project the ripples into unseen space.

title: AI Newsletter #01 – Kolmogorov-Arnold Networks!
text:
A note on initialization
Normal networks “play it safe” and start with tiny weights to keep training stable. But in this case, a sine wave is basically flat around zero. Feed in tiny weights, and every sine in the network acts like a straight line. Your flexible KAN “flatlines” and loses all ability to bend around the data.
The Fix:
Borrowing a trick from SIRENs, we amplify the first layer’s weights, say 10×. This pushes signals out of the flat zone and forces the network to hit sine peaks and valleys from Epoch 0.
The Trade-off:
A hypersensitive, oscillating landscape means learning rates must be precise, if they are too high, the optimizer will most likely bounce away. SIREN-KANs are extremely powerful, but far less forgiving than standard MLPs in this regard. So we had to initialize them multiple times before achieving a good representation!

title: AI Newsletter #01 – Kolmogorov-Arnold Networks!
section: Conclusion and When to Use a KAN
text:
Conclusion and When to Use a KAN
Kolmogorov–Arnold Networks actually feel like a different way of thinking about neural networks. Instead of relying on rigid hyperplanes, they learn flexible one-dimensional functions, which lines up nicely with the Kolmogorov–Arnold theorem. In practice, that means better accuracy, far fewer parameters, and models that are easier to interpret.
The radial ripple experiment makes this pretty clear: about 12× fewer parameters, almost perfect interpolation, and much more stable behavior outside the training range, where a standard MLP tends to fall apart. That’s the core reason KANs (and SIREN-style variants) are getting so much attention.

Final recommendation - Use a KAN when:

You need parameter-efficient approximation of smooth, highly compositional, or periodic physical/symbolic equations.
Interpretability matters — pruning the univariate functions yields human-readable symbolic expressions!
You are operating in low-to-medium input dimensionality \((n \lesssim 20)\).

Do NOT use a KAN when

Input dimensionality is extreme (raw images, text tokens, etc.). The (2n+1) inner-sum expansion becomes a computational bottleneck and standard Transformers or MLPs still dominate here.


Easiest way to see how it works is to clone the repo!

Full reproducible notebook → manswestman/KAN-basics

title: AI Newsletter #02 – Geometric Deep Learning
text:
1. Introduction
Can we derive the neural network architectures from mathematical properties we want it to satisfy, rather than solely relying on engineering intuition? And can such a construction help explain why certain architectures work so well?
In this second CAIS newsletter, we explore these two questions through the lens of Geometric Deep Learning (GDL), a mathematical framework for understanding neural networks through the underlying structure of data. Our primary goal is to show how one of the most influential architectures in deep learning, the Convolutional Neural Network (CNN), can be mathematically derived from simpler geometric principles, and subsequentially explore what this tells us about the broader future of deep learning.

title: AI Newsletter #02 – Geometric Deep Learning
text:
2. Real-world data has structure
There are a lot of deep learning architectures with more and more architectures being invented every week. Each are engineered for different tasks, with different advantages and properties. This vast quantity of architectures can make it extremely difficult to understand why they work and the relations between them.

There is a veritable zoo of neural network architectures for various kinds of data, but few unifying principles. [1]

In their proto-book [1], Bronstein et al. highlight this problem, but also offer a solution: A framework to systemize neural architectures and construct them from geometric regularities. They call it Geometric deep learning (GDL). The idea of GDL rests on an observation in deep learning that the data we care about in the real world isn’t just a collection of random numbers. Instead, it possesses structure, like symmetry, geometry, and other mathematical structures, because it originates from our physical world.
The following is a very import example of this which we will come back to over and over again, so make sure it feels intuitive!
Consider the task of imagine classification where we want to classify cats in images. A physical property could be as simple as recognizing that an object (like a cat in an image) remains the same object whether it is in the top-left corner or the bottom-right corner of the image. This is something that is intuitive for us humans, but not as intuitive for machine learning systems. In traditional deep learning, images are treated as flat grids of pixels, and while architectures like regular Multilayer Perceptrons (MLPs) doesn’t necessarily fail at recognizing a translated cat, it doesn’t enforce any particular relationship between recognizing a cat at one position and recognizing it at another. So it must learn this relationship from data, and so we need more data for this architecture to perform better.
Now imagine a network that detects a particular feature of a cat, such as its ears. If we shift the entire image to the right, we would intuitively expect the network’s detection of those ears to shift to the right as well. The feature of an ear has not changed, only its location. This is the idea behind a geometric property called translation equivariance, which means that translating the input should translate the corresponding output feature maps in the same way. Notice that this is slightly different from what we described in the previous paragraph, and from what we ultimately want in image classification. The final prediction, “cat”, should remain unchanged by translation, a property called translation invariance. But within the network architecture, we want to preserve the location of detected features. This is why translation equivariance is such a useful architectural property, and as we will see, Convolutional Neural Networks (CNNs) are translation-equivariant, and can be derived from translation-equivariant layers.






Figure 1: The left image shows translation-equivariance; if we translate a feature of a cat like its head, the corresponding model representation of it should translate in the same way. The right image shows translation-invariance; translating a cat should not affect the final prediction.



In the framework of GDL, this explains why CNNs are so good at image tasks: They satisfy certain geometric regularities that is very natural to image data. In GDL, regularities refer to geometric properties that we already know are true about the data before the model even starts training. Translation invariance and translation equivariance are only two examples. Some other common regularities which we won’t dive into are rotation invariance/equivariance and permutation invariance/equivariance.
Not only could this allow us to incorporate prior knowledge into neural networks, derive architectures from mathematical principles, and construct more efficient models, but in the long-term lead, it might lead to a shared mathematical framework to study architectures in. It could help explain why some architectures generalize better than others, and help us move deep learning closer to a physical science, rather than just a field of engineering.

title: AI Newsletter #02 – Geometric Deep Learning
text:
3. Mathematical foundations of GDL

3.1 Data domains and signals
Since we want to embrace and utilize the structure within datasets, we want to move away from thinking of data as arbitrary vectors in Euclidean space \(\mathbb{R}^{d}\). Instead, we view data as signals \(x:\Omega\to{}\mathcal{C}\), defined over a data domain \(\Omega\) and mapping into a channel space \(\mathcal{C}\). Some concrete examples are:

For images: \(\Omega=\mathbb{Z}^{2}\), describing a 2D grid, while \(\mathcal{C}=\mathbb{R}^{3}\), describing RGB values. So the signals \(x:\mathbb{Z}^{2}\to{}\mathbb{R}^{3}\) describe a mapping where each pixel at \((i,j)\in{}\mathbb{Z}^{2}\) receives three values \((R,G,B)\in{}\mathbb{R}^{3}\).

Relevant tasks: Image classification, object detection.
Physical structure and priors: Translation, rotation.

For graphs: Let \(G=(V,E)\) be a graph, consisting of vertices \(V\) and edges \(E\). Then \(\Omega=V\), \(\mathcal{C}=\mathbb{R}^{d}\), and signals \(x:V\to{}\mathbb{R}^{d}\) describe a mapping where each node \(n\in{}V\) gets assigned a particular feature or value. For example, in a molecular graph, nodes could be atoms and edges chemical bonds, and signal could assign to each atom its charge, atomic number, mass number, and so on.

Relevant tasks: Molecule generation, predicting whether a molecule possesses certain physical properties, social (user-user relation) recommendations, detecting span accounts.
Physical structure and priors: Locality, node permutation.

For manifolds: Let \(M\) be a smooth two-dimensional surface. Then, \(\Omega=M\), \(\mathcal{C}=\mathbb{R}\), and signals \(x:M\to{}\mathbb{R}\) describe a mapping where each point on the surface \(p\in{}M\) gets assigned a scalar value (e.g., assigning a temperature on the surface of Earth, represented as a sphere \(M=S^{2}\)).

Relevant tasks: Weather prediction, protein folding.
Physical structure and priors: Locality, metric structure describing distances and curvature.


So when we refer to “samples” or “data points” in GDL, we really mean mappings from the data domain to the channel space. The dataset will then be a set of signals, denoted: \[\mathcal{X}(\Omega,\mathcal{C}):=\{ x:\Omega\to{}\mathcal{C} \}.\] This is a way for us to represent data. However, the prior or physical structure comes not merely from the type of the signals, but from the structure we impose on their domain and from how the architecture respects that structure. All of these notions such as “imposing structure” and an architecture “respecting that structure” will be made precise soon.
To give another example of what these geometric regularities might look like. Consider a task on graph data where we want to predict a molecule’s net charge. Our data domain is a graph where vertices are atoms and edges are chemical bonds between atoms. Every atom (or node in our graph) gets assigned a feature vector containing two chemical properties, namely its atomic number and electrical charge. To feed a molecule into a computer algorithm, we are forced to store the signals in matrices. Take a concrete molecule, like \(H_{2}O\), which has three atoms. In a matrix, we might index the two hydrogen atoms first, or the oxygen atom first (or another combination). However, matrix multiplication is not commutative, so for a naive MLP, we might get completely different predictions of properties depending on the ordering of the indexing when we store the atoms as signals in our matrix. This could correspond to absurd physical logic, where, say, a molecule is predicted to be toxic when read from left-to-right, and not toxic when read from right-to-left. Stepping back, we desire a regularity called permutation invariance, meaning that changing the order of the way in which we store the atoms, should not change the final prediction! This is a symmetry because the process of permuting the atoms shouldn’t change the prediction.


3.2 Group theory in GDL
We will now begin formalizing parts of the story we’ve told so far, and we will begin with the concept of “symmetry”. The regularities we have mentioned so far (like translation equivariance) has to do with the concept of symmetry. Symmetry refers to a certain transformation on an object, such that it leaves it unchanged.
Now, the plan is to describe these symmetries in general, and then derive architectures from constraints that respect them. So how do we describe symmetries mathematically? We use groups, specifically, symmetry groups!
A group is a set \(G\) together with a binary relation \(*:G\times G\to{}G\), which we can denote as a structure \((G,*)\), such that:

For any two elements \(g,h\in{}G\), \(g*h\in{}G\).
\(*\) is associative, meaning that for any \(g,h,f\in{}G\),\[(g*h)*f=g*(h*f).\]
There exists a special element \(e\in{}G\), called the identity, such that for any \(g\in{}G\),\[g*e=e*g=g.\]
For every element \(g\in{}G\), there exists an element \(g^{-1}\), called its inverse, such that\[g^{-1}*g=g*g^{-1}=e.\]

In our context, a symmetry group is a concrete group consisting of elements that are real-world transformations, acting on specific objects or mathematical spaces. The most intuitive examples is the symmetry group of an equilateral triangle, which consists of 6 transformations that correspond to 6 motions that map the triangle onto itself:






Figure 2: Illustration of the 6 transformations of the specific symmetry group of a equilateral triangle.





3.3 Understanding equivariance
Using our knowledge of groups we will now give a mathematically rigorous definition of both equivariance and invariance. Groups allow us to describe symmetries generally (whether it is translations, rotations, or permutations), and so we will define a notion of “group equivariance” and “group invariance”. Then, we will see how we derive the convolution operation used in CNNs purely from translation-equivariant linear maps.
Recall our cat example from section 1. An image can be represented as a signal \(x:\Omega\to\mathcal C\), where \(\Omega=\mathbb Z^2\) is a two-dimensional grid of pixel coordinates and \(\mathcal C=\mathbb R^3\) represents the RGB values at each pixel. We want to describe the transformations that shift an image horizontally or vertically. These transformations form a specific group \(G=(\mathbb Z^2,+)\). An element \(g=(a,b)\in G\) represents a translation by \(a\) pixels horizontally and \(b\) pixels vertically. The group operation is addition (performing two translations corresponds to adding their displacement vectors). The identity is \(e=(0,0)\), and every translation \(g=(a,b)\) has an inverse \(g^{-1}=(-a,-b)\) that moves the image back to its original position.
Up until now, we haven’t actually formalized how this group transform an image. All we’ve done is defined the structure of the symmetry itself, not how that symmetry acts on the image data we’re interested in. For this, we introduce a group action. Informally, a group action describes how the elements of a group act as transformations on some space. In our case, we want to specify how translations act on images.
We denote this action by \(\rho\), and define it as: \[(\rho(t)x)(u)=x(u-t),  \] where \(u\in\mathbb Z^2\) is a pixel coordinate and \(x:\mathbb{Z}^{2}\rightarrow{}\mathbb{R}^{3}\) is a signal.
This simply says that, to obtain the pixel value at position \(u\) in the translated image, we look at the original image at position \(u-t\). Consequently, the entire image shifts by \(t\).
Let \(G\) be a symmetry group. A function \(f:\mathcal{X}(\Omega,\mathcal{C})\rightarrow{}\mathcal{X}(\Omega,\mathcal{C})\) is \(G\)-equivariant if \[f(\rho(t)x)=\rho(t)f(x), \tag 1\] for all \(t\in{}G\). \(f\) is called \(G\)-invariant if instead \[f(\rho(t)x)=f(x), \tag 2\] for all \(t\in{}G\).
When we refer to translation equivariance (resp. invariance) we mean the notion of equivariance (resp. invariance) as defined above, but where the group \(G\) is the translation group \(G=(\mathbb Z^2,+)\).
In words, equivariance says that transforming the input and then applying the network must produce the same result as applying the network first and then transforming its output. Invariance says that transforming the input and then applying the network must produce the same result as simply applying the network, without any transformation.
When we say that a “model should respect the geometric regularity”, we are demanding that its architecture respects these sorts of conditions, such as (1) or (2). This brings us to the last central questions: What kinds of neural network layers satisfy these constraints? And how do we construct architectures that satisfy them?
As we will see, if we restrict ourselves to linear layers and require them to be translation equivariant, we arrive naturally at convolution layers. Then, we will compose multiple convolution layers, nonlinearities, and coarsening layers, and finally add a last invariant-map, which will give us the sort of architecture we initially desired in our cat example.

title: AI Newsletter #02 – Geometric Deep Learning
text:
4. The blueprint of GDL
There are four main building blocks of the GDL framework, and we summarize them in the table below:








Building block
Mathematical role
CNN interpretation




Linear equivariant map
Extract information from nearby points while respecting symmetries
Convolutional layers


Nonlinearity
Increase expresiveness
ReLU, Sigmoid


Coarsening (local pooling)
Construct a lower-resolution representation by combining nearby points
Local average/max pooling


Global invariant map
Produce an output unchanged by the chosen group action
Global average/max pooling



We will now break these four building blocks down.

4.1 Linear Equivariant Map
Recall our cat example. If we translate the image, we want the detected features, such as the cat’s ears or its head, to translate in exactly the same way. This motivates constructing neural network layers that are equivariant to the transformations of our data.
The first building block of GDL is therefore a linear equivariant map: a linear transformation \(B\) that respects (See (1)) the action of a symmetry group (in our case, the actions of the translation group): \[B(\rho(t)x)=\rho(t)B(x).\] In the next section we will see that when we require a linear layer to be equivariant to translations, its mathematical structure is constrained to that of a discrete convolution.


4.2 Nonlinearity
Linear transformations alone are not sufficient to construct expressive neural networks. This is the same story that goes for any neural network; composing any number of linear transformations still produces a linear transformation, which in turn limits the kinds of functions the network can represent. We therefore introduce nonlinear activation functions, such as ReLU or sigmoid. We represent these as \(\boldsymbol\sigma:\mathcal{C}\rightarrow{}\mathcal{C}'\), applied element-wise: \[(\boldsymbol \sigma (x))(u)=\sigma(x(u)).\] Importantly, these nonlinearities preserve translation equivariance. Thus, we can introduce nonlinearity (which drastically improves the expressiveness of our network) without sacrificing the equivariance constraint we imposed on our architecture. For a quick proof of this, see below:
\[
\begin{align}
(\boldsymbol\sigma(\rho(t)x))(u)&=\sigma((\rho(t)x)(u)) \\
&=\sigma(x(u-t)) \\
&=(\boldsymbol\sigma (x))(u-t) \\
&=(\rho(t)\boldsymbol\sigma (x))(u),
\end{align}
\]
hence, we get that \(\boldsymbol\sigma\) is \(G\)-equivariant: \[\boldsymbol\sigma \circ{}\rho(t)=\rho(t)\circ{}\boldsymbol\sigma.\]


4.3 Coarsening
The idea of the coarsening is to construct a new, lower-dimensional domain \(\Omega'\) that represents the original domain at a coarser resolution. Formally, it takes the form \(P:\mathcal{X}(\Omega,\mathcal{C})\rightarrow{}\mathcal{X}(\Omega',\mathcal{C})\) where \(\Omega'\) is the coarsened domain. The average pooling layers in CNNs are examples of coarsening operators. Let \(B_{w}\subseteq{}\Omega\) denote the neighborhood associated with a coarse-grid position \(w\in{}\Omega'\), and define average pooling by: \[P(x)(w)=\frac{1}{|B_{w}|}\sum_{u\in{}B_{w}}x(u).\]






Figure 3: An illustration of an average pooling layer.



But why should we desire coarsening anyways? The reason for this is quite intuitive! Suppose we want to classify cats in images again. At the finest scale, we observe individual pixels. But at coarser scales, we observe edges, textures, shapes, and arrangements of features like ears, paws, noses, and so on. The key observation here is that many real-world tasks possess structure at multiple spatial scales. Rather than processing all information globally at once, we can exploit this by constructing local features and progressively combining them into coarser representations. In other words, not every tiny local variation is usually essential to the prediction. For example, a small change in a cat’s fur texture might leave the correct class unchanged. This suggests that useful information may be represented at multiple resolutions, with some fine-scale details discarded as we move toward coarser scales.
This idea is captured in another geometric regularity used in GDL, which is referred to as scale separation. Formally, if \(P_{j}:\mathcal{X}(\Omega)\rightarrow{}\mathcal{X}_{j}(\Omega_{j})\) is a coarsening operator, and \(f\) is our network, then we assume \[f \approx f_{j}\circ{}P_{j},\] where \(f_{j}\) is a function operating on the coarser domain. Intuitively, this means we can approximately perform the original task using the coarsened representation \(P_{j}(x)\) instead of the original high-resolution signal \(x\). Note that this is an assumption about the structure of the task. It makes sense for our cat example. However, another task requiring the exact value of one particular pixel might not benefit at all from scale separation.


4.4 Global Pooling
Returning once again to our cat example, recall the distinction between equivariance and invariance. Within the network, we want detected features to move when the input image moves. However, the final prediction should remain unchanged: a cat is still a cat regardless of where it appears in the image. This is precisely the role of the last ingredient we need: A final global pooling layer.
Suppose one of our final feature maps indicates where the network has detected a particular feature of the cat. By having imposed translation equivariance (from section 4.1), translating the image will also translate the positions where this feature is detected. But if we aggregate the feature values across the entire data domain, their locations no longer matter. The resulting representation can therefore be translation-invariant!
Unlike local pooling, global pooling is constructed such that it produces a representation that no longer depends on the spatial position of a feature. Suppose our final convolutional layer produces a feature map \(h:\Omega\to\mathbb R^C\) where each spatial position has a vector of \(C\) learned features. One example of a global pooling layer would be the global average, which computes: \[A(h)=\frac{1}{|\Omega|}\sum_{u\in{}\Omega}h(u).\] The result is a single vector in \(\mathbb{R}^{C}\), rather than a spatial feature map. Now, recall our translation group \((\mathbb{Z}_{2},+)\) with action \(\rho\). Then:
\[
\begin{align}
A(\rho(t)h)&=\frac{1}{|\Omega|}\sum_{u\in{}\Omega} h(u-t) \\
&= \frac{1}{|\Omega|}\sum_{u\in{}\Omega}h(u) \\
&=A(h).
\end{align}
\]
This is exactly the invariance condition in (2)! The second equality follows from the fact that translations change the positions of feature values, but not the values themselves, so it doesn’t affect the global average. Thus, global pooling turns a translation-equivariant feature representation into a translation-invariant output, which is exactly what we wanted for the cat-classification problem (recall image 1)!
There is one technical remark. The expression for \(A(h)\) is typically not defined for \(\Omega=\mathbb{Z}^{2}\) since this set is infinite. To overcome this we use a finite periodic grid, such as \(\Omega=\mathbb Z_H\times\mathbb Z_W\), with translations interpreted periodically. But the mathematical representation is the same. For more details, see section 4.2 of [1].
So global pooling allows us to move from equivariant representations, which preserve spatial information, to invariant representations, which discard positional information when it is no longer needed for the task.


4.5 The general blueprint of GDL
Putting these building blocks together, we have a sort of “blueprint” for deriving deep learning architectures that satisfy geometric regularities. In the context of our cat example:

Start with an input image \(x:\Omega \rightarrow{}\mathbb{R}^{3}\).
Apply a local equivariant layer \(B\), followed up by a nonlinearity \(\boldsymbol\sigma\). This step extracts local features in a way that respects the symmetry we impose.
(optional) Combine nearby information via a coarsening operator (local average pooling) on a smaller domain.
Repeat local equivariant operations with nonlinearities, and optionally coarsenings.
Finally, aggregate features into a position-independent representation, via a global invariant map \(A\) (global average map).

Note that from step 3, we keep composing local equivariant layers followed up by nonlinearities. But so far, we only know that each are equivariant separately, but is their composition also equivariant? That is, we know \(B\) is equivariant by definition, and we’ve proven that \(\boldsymbol\sigma\) is equivariant in section 4.2, but is \(\boldsymbol \sigma \circ{} B\) also equivariant then? We verify that this is indeed the case, and this is our last technical detail for this section:
\[
\begin{align}
(\boldsymbol\sigma\circ{}B)(\rho(t)x)&=\boldsymbol\sigma(B(\rho(t)x))  \\
&=\boldsymbol\sigma(\rho(t)B(x)) &\text{(equivariance of }B\text{)}\\
&=\rho(t)\boldsymbol\sigma(B(x)) &\text{(equivariance of }\rho\text{)}\\
&=\rho(t)(\boldsymbol\sigma \circ{}B)(x)
\end{align}
\]
This is why we can construct deep nonlinear networks that remain translation-equivariant by design. We can alternate convolutions and pointwise nonlinearities, gaining expressive power while preserving the equivariance constraints, which is a wonderful thing to have!
In all its generality, independent of task, data domain, or group, the Geometric Deep Learning Blueprint is formulated as follows: Let \(\Omega\) and \(\Omega'\) be domains, \(G\) a symmetry group over \(\Omega\), and write \(\Omega' \subseteq \Omega\) if \(\Omega'\) can be considered a compact version of \(\Omega\). Then we have the following building blocks:

Linear \(G\)-equivariant layer \(B :\mathcal X( \Omega, \mathcal C)\to \mathcal X ( \Omega ' , \mathcal C')\) satisfying \(B(g\cdot x)=g\cdot B(x)\) for all \(g\in G\) and \(x\in \mathcal X(\Omega, \mathcal C)\).
Nonlinearity \(\sigma:\mathcal C \to \mathcal C'\) applied element-wise as \((\boldsymbol \sigma(x))(u)=\sigma(x(u))\).
Local pooling (coarsening) \(P:\mathcal X( \Omega, \mathcal C)\to \mathcal X(\Omega' ,\mathcal C)\), such that \(\Omega' \subseteq \Omega\).
\(G\)-invariant layer (global pooling) \(A:\mathcal X(\Omega, \mathcal C)\to \mathcal Y\) satisfying \(A(g\cdot x)=A(x)\) for all \(g\in G\) and \(x\in X(\Omega, \mathcal C)\).

Using these blocks allows constructing \(G\)-invariant functions \(f:\mathcal X(\Omega, \mathcal C)\to \mathcal Y\) of the form \[f=A\circ \boldsymbol \sigma_J \circ B_j \circ P_{J-1}\circ \dots \circ P_1\circ \boldsymbol \sigma_1 \circ B_1,\] where the blocks are selected such that the output space of each block matches the input space of the next one. Here we assume the intermediate operators like local pooling layers also preserve the relevant equivariance constraints. Different blocks may exploit different choices of symmetry groups \(G\).

title: AI Newsletter #02 – Geometric Deep Learning
section: 5. Deriving Convolutional Neural Networks from Translation Equivariance
text:
5. Deriving Convolutional Neural Networks from Translation Equivariance
We now have all the mathematical tools necessary to return to our original question: Can we derive the architecture of a neural network from the geometric properties we want it to satisfy?
Recall that we represented images as signals on a two-dimensional grid \(\Omega=\mathbb Z^2\), and established that we want our intermediate layers to be translation equivariant. But what does this requirement actually tell us about how the layers themselves must be constructed?
Rather than starting with a convolutional layer and verifying that it is equivariant, we will start with an arbitrary linear layer, impose translation equivariance, and investigate what this forces! As we will see, this leads directly to convolution, and provides a principled explanation for one of the defining operations of CNNs.

5.1 Convolution emerges from translation symmetry
Consider a linear layer \(B\), which can be written in terms of weights \(W(u,v)\) as follows: \[(Bx)(u)=\sum_{v\in{}\mathbb{Z}^{2}}W(u,v)x(v),\] where \(v\) is an input pixel position, \(u\) is an output pixel position, and \(W(u,v)\) is the weight connecting input position \(v\) to output position \(u\). At this point, the weights are completely unconstrained. But from our GDL blueprint, we want \(B\) to respect our translation symmetry, meaning we want \(B\) to be translation equivariant. This meant that: \[B\circ{}\rho(t)=\rho(t)\circ{}B\iff B(\rho(t)x)=\rho(t)(Bx).\tag 3\] We now want to understand what this symmetry constraint tells us about the structure of our weights. Unpacking the left-hand side of (3), we get: \[(B(\rho(t)x))(u)=\sum_{v\in{}\mathbb{Z}^{2}}W(u,v)(\rho(t)x)(v)=\sum_{v\in{}\mathbb{Z}^{2}}W(u,v)x(v-t).\] Unpacking the right-hand side of (3), we get: \[(\rho(t)(Bx))(u)=(Bx)(u-t)=\sum_{v\in{}\mathbb{Z}^{2}}W(u-t,v)x(v).\] Therefore, equivariance tells us that: \[\sum_{v\in{}\mathbb{Z}^{2}}W(u,v)x(v-t)=\sum_{v\in{}\mathbb{Z}^{2}}W(u-t,v)x(v).\] Because we want both sides to have \(x\) evaluated at the same index so that we can compare the weights, we now make a reindexing of the sum in the left-hand side using \(w:=v-t\) (so \(v=w+t\)), which doesn’t change the sum. Thus, we get: \[\sum_{w\in{}\mathbb{Z}^{2}}W(u,w+t)x(w)=\sum_{w\in{}\mathbb{Z}^{2}}W(u-t,w)x(w).\] Consequently, \[W(u,w+t)=W(u-t,w),\] and finally, we substitute \(u\) by \(u+t\) to get: \[W(u+t,w+t)=W(u,w).\tag 4\]
You might know about weight-sharing, which traditionally is said to be a “design technique” in machine learning that forces layers to share parameters (such as weights). Equation (4) is weight-sharing, but it is no longer an arbitrary design principle, but a genuine consequence of translation equivariance! This already hints at the explanatory power of GDL.
Equation (4) says that if we want our linear layers \(B\) to be equivariant to translations, then moving the input and output positions by the same displacement must not change the weight connecting them.
From (4), choose the particular translation \(t=-w\). Then, \[W(u-w,0)=W(u,w).\tag 5\] This translates both positions so that the input position becomes the origin \(0=(0,0)\). Because equivariance tells us that the weight is unchanged by simultaneous translation, every weight can be recovered by looking at weights whose input position is the origin. This is how we define the kernel \(k(s)\), which is the weight connecting the input at the origin to the output at a displacement \(s\): \[k(s):=W(s,0)\] The symmetry constraint has allowed us to replace a function of two positions \(W:\mathbb{Z}^{2}\times \mathbb{Z}^{2}\rightarrow{}\mathbb{R}\) with a function of one relative displacement \(k:\mathbb{Z}^{2}\rightarrow{}\mathbb{R}\)! Using (5) and the definition of \(k(s)\), \[W(u,w)=k(u-w)\] Substituting this into our original linear layer \(B\): \[(Bx)(u)=\sum_{v\in{}\mathbb{Z}^{2}}W(u,v)x(v)=\sum_{v\in{}\mathbb{Z}^{2}}k(u-v)x(v)=(k*x)(u). \tag 6\] This is exactly the definition of the (discrete) convolution operation from which convolutional layers literally get their name from!
We have now derived convolution directly from linearity and translation equivariance. If you want to learn more about the convolution operation itself, which would give a higher appreciation for what we have just done, see [2].


5.2 Deriving the traditional CNN architecture
In the previous section we showed that linearity and translation equivariance force a layer to take the form of a convolution. But so far, we have only derived a single linear operator. How can we use this result to construct an entire neural network architecture? Using our blueprint at the beginning of section 4.2, we are only done with step 0 and step 1 at this point. But before we continue with step 2, we need to discuss two technical details.
In the derivation of (6), we used scalar-valued signals \(x:\mathbb{Z}^{2}\rightarrow{}\mathbb{R}\), but our original cat example involves RGB images \(x:\mathbb{Z}^{2}\rightarrow{}\mathbb{R}^{3}\). So first, we generalize slightly: Suppose an input image has \(3\) channels and the output has \(N\) channels, then each output channel \(j\) can be calculated by: \[(Bx)_{j}(u)=\sum_{c=1}^{3}\sum_{s \in{}K}k_{jc}(s)x_{c}(u-s),\] where \(k_{jc}\) is the kernel connecting input channel \(c\) with output channel \(j\).
Another technicality is that translation equivariance alone does not force the kernel to be local. The function \(k\) as constructed in section 5.1 could assign nonzero weights to arbitrarily large displacements. To obtain the usual CNN filters, such as a standard \(3\times3\) kernel, we impose locality. We say that \(k(s)=0\) whenever \(s\not\in K\), where \(K\subseteq{}\mathbb{Z}^{2}\) is a small neighborhood around the origin.
Now, we assemble our CNN! Let \(h^{(0)}=x\) denote the input signal. We construct feature maps using: \[h^{(l+1)}=\sigma_{l}(B_{l}h^{(l)}),\] where \(B_{l}\) is our convolution operator, \(\sigma_{l}\) is our nonlinearity, and \(l\) is an index denoting the layer of our network. We’ve already proven that both operators are translation equivariant (See section 4.2) and that their composition is also translation equivariant (See section 4.5). Thus, \(h^{(l+1)}\) is also translation equivariant. This was step 2 in the blueprint.
We can also insert intermediate coarsenings \(P_{l}\), giving instead: \[h^{(l+1)}=P_{l}(B_{l}(h^{(l)})).\] However, this might not always preserve equivariance. Coarsening may preserve only a subgroup of translations, or an appropriate weaker equivariance property.
We are now at the last step of our blueprint! Suppose we now have constructed several equivariant convolutional layers, giving an overall architecture \[E=\boldsymbol{\sigma}_{l}\circ{}B_{l}\circ{}\dots \circ{}\boldsymbol{\sigma}_{2}\circ{}B_{2}\circ{}\boldsymbol{\sigma}_{1}\circ{}B_{1}.\] We know \(E\) is translation-equivariant. But by step 4, we require an invariant predictor, and so we require a translation-invariant global pooling layer. We already know global average pooling \(A\) is translation-invariant (See section 4.4), and so our final CNN model is: \[f_{\text{CNN}}=A\circ{}E.\] We’ve now constructed a translation-invariant image classifier from translation-equivariant convolutional layers!

title: AI Newsletter #02 – Geometric Deep Learning
text:
6. Conclusions and final reflections
We began this newsletter by asking whether we can derive neural architectures from mathematical constraints, and whether doing so can explain why they work. We have now given an answer of the first question: by requiring linearity and translation equivariance, we derived convolution, and from there constructed the familiar CNN architecture using the GDL blueprint. But the second question is maybe the more interesting one, and remains much more mysterious.
Building a CNN in PyTorch is certainly easier than deriving one mathematically like we did here. Yet, there is something fundamentally different about these two approaches. Much of modern deep learning has been shaped by empirical discoveries and engineering principles. We have found effective architectures often before fully understanding why they work, when they generalize, how they relate to other architectures, and when one architecture is preferable to another. We have not answered all of these questions, but we have shown how GDL offers something important. An explanation for why convolution and weight sharing are natural choices for data with translation symmetry.
GDL offers a method for how we might move beyond simply discovering architectures that work, toward understanding the mathematics that make them work. It is not a complete theory of modern deep learning, but a useful step toward one.

title: AI Newsletter #03 – Learning to predict fluid motion with Fourier neural operators
text:
When we started this project, we found that most information about operator learning was quite abstract and difficult to connect to an actual implementation. We wanted to understand the mathematical foundations of Fourier neural operators (FNOs) well enough to build one from scratch and then also learn how to apply it to a real problem.
We also wrote a full report (PDF) that aims to build intuition around the underlying theory, from operators and kernels to our implementation and results. Essentially, we wanted to write the resource that we would have liked to have when we were getting started to get off the ground more quickly. The code is also available on GitHub.
If it feels a bit much to read through the full report, this newsletter is meant to serve as a high-level overview. We walk through why standard neural networks struggle with continuous fields, how a few simple mathematical symmetries make the problem much more intuitive, and what we found when comparing our model to a numerical solver.

title: AI Newsletter #03 – Learning to predict fluid motion with Fourier neural operators
text:
Predicting continuous fields
Many engineering problems involve predicting fields across space, such as temperature distributions, structural deformation, or fluid motion. Numerical solvers calculate how these change over time by dividing space into a grid and taking small steps forward in time. However, to keep the simulation stable and prevent errors from blowing up, solvers have to take very small steps. Repeating this for different designs or initial conditions can quickly become expensive.
Instead, a trained surrogate model (like an FNO) offers an alternative approach with the aim of speeding up this process. First, we can use a solver to generate example data, train a network to learn how the system behaves (the underlying dynamics), and then reuse that model for faster predictions.
The problem we applied this to was 2D fluid dynamics (under the Navier-Stokes equations), specifically predicting the evolution of vorticity—a scalar field describing how much the fluid rotates at each point.






Figure 1: Twenty-frame forecast on a 256×256 grid. The numerical ground truth is on the left, our FNO prediction in the middle, and the absolute error on the right.



The first challenge one is faced with when trying to solve this problem is how to represent a fluid state in a neural network.
On a \(64 \times 64\) grid, we have 4,096 numbers describing the state. The most straightforward approach is to place those numbers into a vector and feed them into a standard Multi-Layer Perceptron (MLP). But this approach has two main issues:

Lost spatial geometry: Flattening the field into a vector ignores (and removes) spatial relationships. This means that points that sit next to each other in the fluid can end up far apart in a 1D vector. In other words, the network does not automatically know that pixel \((1, 64)\) is right next to pixel \((2, 64)\).
Resolution lock-in: An MLP is fundamentally tied to the number of input nodes. If you train on 4,096 numbers and then want to evaluate the same fluid on a finer \(256 \times 256\) grid (65,536 values), the matrix multiplications do not match in size. (So this is just an impossibility, not a matter of accuracy.)

You might have heard of Convolutional neural networks (CNNs) before (especially if you have read our previous newsletter!) and it is quite intuitive that they can handle spatial relationships much better than traditional MLPs. However, standard CNN filters are tied to pixel steps rather than physical distances, and their receptive fields are local, meaning that they focus on a small area at a time. In a fluid, what happens at one side of the domain affects the other side. So, in essence this means that it is not very natural for a CNN to connect distant points and their interaction (this is the theory of priors).
The core issue is that a fluid is not really a list of numbers but is actually a continuous field, and the grid that we give a network is just where we happened to measure that field.

title: AI Newsletter #03 – Learning to predict fluid motion with Fourier neural operators
text:
From vectors to operators
A field can be thought of as a function in 3D space that looks like a surface with hills and valleys. This means that to build a model that is not tied to one grid resolution and can model fields, we need a mapping that takes an entire function as input and outputs a function. In mathematics, a mapping between functions is called an operator.
Differentiation (\(\frac{d}{dx}\)) is a familiar example of a linear operator: you feed in a function like \(f(x) = x^2\), and it returns another function, \(f'(x) = 2x\).
When we try to solve this problem we do something similar conceptually but now we take an initial fluid field and map it to a fluid field at a future time. That mapping is a solution operator.
This would mean that if we can train a neural network to approximate this underlying operator (relatively well), the model becomes grid-independent. We can train it on whichever grid resolution is fast to simulate, and then evaluate it on a different grid without changing the network weights.
Essentially, we try to learn the underlying physics so that we can look at the function anywhere, as it is continuous, and not just at the points we happened to sample it.

title: AI Newsletter #03 – Learning to predict fluid motion with Fourier neural operators
text:
Kernels and symmetries
The idea of learning a mapping between functions can sound abstract at first. How do you actually design a neural network layer that acts on a continuous function instead of a discrete vector?
In a standard linear layer, the output at a given point is a weighted sum over all input points, using a weight matrix \(W\). To turn this into a continuous operation, we can replace the matrix with an integral kernel which basically is a function \(K(x, y)\) that describes the weight connecting input position \(y\) to output position \(x\):
\[(\mathcal{K}v)(x) = \int K(x, y) \, v(y) \, dy\]
In an ordinary neural network, it has to learn a separate weight for every connection in a matrix. However, if you have an infinite number of continuous points, that would mean learning an infinite number of weights! But what if we can use symmetric properties from the actual physics of the field…

1. Relative displacement and convolution
In a fluid, the physical interaction between two points typically depends on their relative displacement, i.e., how far apart they are and in what direction. That is, the distance between them is more important than their absolute coordinates:
\[K(x, y) = \kappa(x - y)\]
If the weights depend only on displacement, moving the output point simply shifts the weighting pattern across the domain. Applying this same shifted pattern everywhere is exactly what is called convolution.
You can think of this as a rule that we slide across the input field, and applying this to each pair of points based on how far apart they are. This means that any point can interact with any other point and the rule changes based on their relative position.


2. Why Fourier space speeds this up
A global convolution across \(N\) grid points connects every point to every other point. Computing this directly in physical space requires \(O(N^2)\) operations, which quickly becomes expensive on finer grids.
This is where Fourier transforms help. Instead of describing the fluid point by point, we can describe it as a sum of sine and cosine waves across the domain. Broad waves describe large flows, while finer waves describe smaller, oscillating variations.
The reason this helps is a central property of convolution: it preserves frequency. When you apply convolution to a sine wave, the output remains a sine wave with the exact same frequency—only its amplitude (magnitude) and phase (shift) change.
This is the crucial part, because waves of different frequencies do not mix during convolution: - We do not need to calculate all pairwise interactions across space. - We can transform the field into Fourier space with a Fast Fourier Transform (FFT), adjust each wave’s amplitude and phase by multiplying with learned complex weights, and transform back with an inverse FFT. - Using the FFT, the computational cost drops from \(O(N^2)\) to \(O(N \log N)\).
On top of that, in fluid dynamics, most of the field’s behavior is captured by the lower-frequency waves that drives the flow. Therefore, we can simply cut off some of the higher frequencies and keep the lowest modes (in our case, the first 12 frequencies along each axis). This keeps the number of learned parameters relatively small while still capturing most of the dynamics of the flow.

title: AI Newsletter #03 – Learning to predict fluid motion with Fourier neural operators
text:
Transferring to higher resolutions
Because the learned weights are associated with specific wave frequencies rather than grid indices, they are not tied to the resolution used during training.
We trained our model on trajectories simulated at \(64 \times 64\). Once trained, we ran the exact same model weights on a \(256 \times 256\) grid—sixteen times as many points—without any fine-tuning or retraining.
As shown in the rollout animation above, the model produces a coherent forecast on the finer grid. The mean per-step error on \(256 \times 256\) was close to the error on the coarse grid, even though it had never seen that resolution during training!
This is called zero-shot super-resolution and it is one of the best demonstrations of what operator learning is able to do.

title: AI Newsletter #03 – Learning to predict fluid motion with Fourier neural operators
text:
What we learned
While the properties of FNOs sound good in theory, building and profiling the model also gave us a better view of the practical trade-offs compared to traditional numerical solvers:

Speed: On the \(64 \times 64\) grid, our FNO was about 5 times faster than our numerical solver using the largest stable time step we could take. On the \(256 \times 256\) grid, the speedup increased to roughly 13 times (and up to ~80 times when comparing against smaller solver time steps).
Batching: Unlike traditional solvers that usually simulate one trajectory at a time, the neural network processes batches very efficiently. In our test, predicting 8 or 16 trajectories at once gave a substantial throughput gain without much added latency.
Accuracy and rollout drift: The numerical solver was still noticeably more accurate. In our setup, the model predicted 20 steps into the future autoregressively, feeding each output back in as the input for the next step. As time progresses, small per-step errors compound, and the small details in the vorticity field gradually become softer than in the numerical simulation.
When it might be useful: Generating training data and training the network requires compute, and a surrogate model only makes practical sense if you plan to make enough predictions afterward to offset that initial cost, such as in real-time control, interactive design, or large parameter studies. Additionally, when speed is more important than accuracy, the FNO can be a good option. For example, in a real-time control application, you might want to quickly evaluate many different control strategies and then pick the best one to implement.

title: AI Newsletter #03 – Learning to predict fluid motion with Fourier neural operators
text:
Conclusion and takeaways
These are some of the key takeaways from exploring the mathematical foundations and implementation of the FNO:

Continuous fields: When a problem is of a continuous nature or does not have a natural concept of a “pixel”, using operator theory avoids having to design the architecture around a specific resolution.
Kernels and convolution: Because points interact based on their relative distance rather than where they sit in space, we can slide a single “interaction rule” across the whole fluid. This gives every point a direct way to interact with every other point through a global convolution.
Fourier shortcut: Because convolution preserves wave frequencies, working in the frequency domain makes global interactions much more computationally feasible and also allows filtering out high-frequency noise.
Resolution transfer: When network weights represent operations on physical frequencies and approximate a field to field mapping, the model generalizes across resolutions naturally.

If you want to explore the mathematical derivations in detail, the numerical solver setup, or our implementation details, you can find them in our full report (PDF) and the GitHub repository.
We thank our partner Aixia for providing the AiQu computing resources used for training.

title: AI Newsletter #03 – Learning to predict fluid motion with Fourier neural operators
section: What we learned: speed versus accuracy
text:
What we learned: speed versus accuracy
While the properties of FNOs sound good in theory, building and profiling the model also gave us a better view of the practical trade-offs compared to traditional numerical solvers:

Speed: On the \(64 \times 64\) grid, our FNO was about 5 times faster than our numerical solver using the largest stable time step we could take. On the \(256 \times 256\) grid, the speedup increased to roughly 13 times (and up to ~80 times when comparing against smaller solver time steps).

Accuracy and rollout drift: The numerical solver was still noticeably more accurate. In our setup, the model predicted 20 steps into the future autoregressively, feeding each output back in as the input for the next step. As time progresses, small per-step errors compound, and the small details in the vorticity field gradually become softer than in the numerical simulation.
When it might be useful: Generating training data and training the network requires compute, and a surrogate model only makes practical sense if you plan to make enough predictions afterward to offset that initial cost, such as in real-time control, interactive design, or large parameter studies. Additionally, when speed is more important than accuracy, the FNO can be a good option. For example, in a real-time control application, you might want to quickly evaluate many different control strategies and then pick the best one to implement.
